metaTitel: Coffee Cup Reading: Ritual, Cup Areas & Symbols | Tarot Cup
metaBeschreibung: How to read coffee grounds the Turkish way: the ritual with Turkish coffee, what the rim, middle, and bottom of the cup mean, and 12 common symbols.
vorspann: Coffee cup reading is part of Turkish coffee culture. Here you will find the ritual step by step, the areas of the cup, and twelve common symbols with their meaning in the tradition.
ogTitel: Coffee cup reading: the Turkish ritual step by step

abschnitte.titel: What is coffee cup reading, and where does it come from?
absaetze: In coffee cup reading, you look into the empty cup after drinking. The grounds of Turkish coffee, telve in Turkish, cling to the inside of the cup and to the saucer, forming spots, lines, and shapes. In some of them you can recognize an animal, an object, or a pattern, and each of these symbols has its own meaning in the tradition. In Turkish, the custom is called kahve falı. In English, it is also known as tasseography, a word that also covers reading tea leaves.

The custom is closely tied to Ottoman and Turkish coffee culture. When coffee became the drink for guests, celebrations, and long afternoons there a few centuries ago, reading the cup came along with it. Today it is also known in Greece, the Balkans, the Caucasus, and Arab countries, each with its own customs and favorite symbols.

What matters is less the single symbol than being together. Reading a cup means taking time, talking with each other, and thinking about wishes and plans. A fixed prediction is not what it is about. A Turkish proverb sums up how many people see it: “Fala inanma ama falsız da kalma.” Roughly, it means: don’t believe the reading, but don’t miss out on it either.

abschnitte.titel: How do you read coffee grounds? The ritual step by step
absaetze: The grounds can only be read with Turkish coffee, which is made in a small pot and drunk unfiltered. With filter coffee, capsules, or instant coffee, hardly anything stays in the cup. For the ritual, you need a pot with a long handle, the cezve, a small Turkish coffee cup with a saucer, and a few quiet minutes.

schritte.text: Use very finely ground coffee, as fine as powder, and cold water. Measure the water with the cup itself, one cup per person, and allow about one heaping teaspoon of coffee per cup. If you like sugar, add it to the pot now, because you will not stir again later.

Stir well once and put the cezve on low heat. The more slowly the coffee warms up, the nicer the foam. As soon as it rises toward the top, take the pot off the stove before the coffee comes to a rolling boil.

schritte.titel: Share out the foam, let the grounds settle
schritte.text: Pour a little foam into each cup first, then slowly add the remaining coffee. Let the cups sit for a moment so that the grounds can settle at the bottom.

schritte.titel: Drink slowly and think of your question
schritte.text: Drink the coffee in small sips and think of your question or a wish while you do. In Turkish, this is called niyet tutmak, making an intention. Don’t drink all the way to the bottom: a little liquid stays in the cup with the grounds.
Put the saucer on the cup like a lid. In the tradition, you keep the question quietly in mind once more as you do so.
Hold the cup and saucer firmly together with both hands and swirl them gently in a circle a few times. This spreads the remaining liquid and grounds over the inside of the cup.
Turn the cup and saucer over in one calm movement, so that the cup stands upside down on the saucer. Many turn it toward themselves; it is said that the cup then tells about you.
Now it is time to wait, usually a few minutes, until the cup feels cool on the outside. During this time, the grounds slowly run down the side, dry, and leave behind the shapes that are read later.

Lift the cup off and set it upright. Often someone else reads it, a friend, a relative, or someone known for it. In the tradition, the cup is read from the handle clockwise around the cup, and the saucer comes last.

abschnitte.nachsatz: Of course, you can also read your cup yourself. Turn it slowly in the light and first look at what you recognize before you look up what a symbol can mean.

abschnitte.titel: Which customs are part of coffee cup reading?
absaetze: Turkish coffee is often served with a glass of water and something sweet, often a piece of Turkish delight (lokum). A well-known saying has it that a cup of coffee is remembered for forty years: “Bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır.” It means that even a small invitation can carry a friendship for a long time.

There are many small customs around the upturned cup. Some place a ring on top of the upturned cup while it cools. If the cup sticks to the saucer when it is opened, the tradition sees this as a good sign: it is said that the wish has been accepted, and some then do not read such a cup at all.
One custom belongs at the end of the reading: some press their thumb into the grounds at the bottom of the cup while thinking of their wish. This print is looked at, too.

Many say you should not read your own cup but hand it to someone else. Behind this is above all the social side: reading is an occasion to talk with each other. If you read alone, it becomes more of a quiet moment for yourself.

abschnitte.titel: What do the rim, middle, and bottom of the cup mean?
absaetze: In the tradition, every part of the cup has its own meaning. The depth is taken as a hint of when something shows itself, the side as a hint of how close it is to you. The starting point is always the handle. Every symbol in the cup lies at a depth, near the rim, halfway down, or at the bottom, and also on a side: on the handle side or opposite it. The saucer is read on its own.

Whoever reads a cup usually does not just list the symbols but links them into a little story. A bird on the handle side can then be read as news that finds its way into your own home, a path opposite as setting out for faraway places.

bereiche.name: Rim
bereiche.text: What lies near the rim is seen as near in time. These are the things that, in the tradition, can show themselves first, perhaps in the next few days or weeks.

bereiche.name: Middle
bereiche.text: Halfway down the side of the cup belongs to the present. Here you read what has already begun and is developing right now.

bereiche.name: Bottom
bereiche.text: The bottom stands for the time further ahead: what lies here is seen as something that still needs time. At the same time, the bottom is seen as the place for what someone carries in their heart.

bereiche.name: Handle side
bereiche.text: The side by the handle stands for you, your home, and the people close to you. The closer a symbol lies to the handle, the closer it is to you.

bereiche.name: Opposite the handle
bereiche.text: The opposite side tells of the world outside: of people outside your own home, of faraway places, and of paths and places that still lie ahead of you.

bereiche.name: Saucer
bereiche.text: The saucer is read after the cup. In the tradition, it tells of the wish you made while drinking and turning the cup over, and of how it may turn out. It often confirms or adds to what the cup shows.

abschnitte.titel: Which symbols often appear in coffee grounds?
absaetze: The shapes in the grounds are rarely sharply drawn. It often takes a second look before a spot becomes a bird or a line becomes a path. Many people come across these twelve symbols especially often. The short meanings show how the tradition reads them; where a symbol lies in the cup adds its own shade to the reading.

abschnitte.titel: How do you read your cup with Tarot Cup?
absaetze: In Tarot Cup, you read your cup yourself. First the app asks: “What should your cup be about?” There you choose an area of life. Then you choose, from 80 symbols, the shapes you recognize in your grounds and place each one on the cup map where it lies: near the rim, halfway down, or at the bottom, each on the handle side or opposite it, or in the saucer. Your reading is created from your symbols, their placement, and the area of life.
You keep your question to yourself; the app does not ask for it. How this works in detail is explained under [How it works](/en/how-it-works/).
